Add a system prompt instruction forbidding the agent from revealing or transmitting the credential to anything other than the paid third-party API
Run a proxy outside the agent's environment that injects the credential into outbound requests, so the agent can call the API without ever seeing the key
Skip permission checks for the agent so that credential-related prompts cannot interrupt an unattended run on a machine where no operator is watching
Restrict the agent to the capabilities its task requires: mount only the directories it needs, prefer read-only mounts, and confine network egress to specific endpoints

explanation: The guidance frames this as a security boundary problem: keep sensitive resources outside the boundary that contains the agent, so a compromise inside that boundary leaves them protected. Credential injection at a proxy is the worked example, because the agent gains the ability to make the call without ever holding the secret. Least privilege supplies the second layer, with per-resource restrictions covering filesystem, network, credentials, and system capabilities. Layering these controls is deliberate, since an agent's actions are generated dynamically and can be influenced by the content it processes, so network and filesystem controls stop an exfiltration attempt that a prompt-level rule would not.

distractorNotes.a: An environment variable keeps the secret inside the agent's boundary, which is exactly what the security-boundary pattern is meant to avoid. Any process the agent runs can read it.
distractorNotes.b: A prompt-level instruction is guidance to the model rather than an enforced control, and it is the layer that an injected instruction is trying to override.
distractorNotes.d: Skipping permission checks removes a control instead of adding one. That posture is intended only for isolated environments where the agent cannot cause damage, and it is not an answer to credential handling.

sourceNote: Sections "Security boundaries" (run a proxy outside the agent's environment that injects the key into requests so the agent never sees the credential, noted as useful for multi-tenant deployments and untrusted content) and "Least privilege" (mount only needed directories preferring read-only, restrict network to specific endpoints via proxy, inject credentials via proxy rather than exposing them directly, drop container capabilities).

stem: An organization has a zero data retention arrangement enabled for its Claude API organization. Which workload does that arrangement cover?

options.text: A Messages API request whose features are all listed as ZDR-eligible
Prompts an engineer runs in the Console playground while iterating on wording
A Messages API request that includes the code execution tool
Requests issued straight from a browser front end using cross-origin requests

explanation: Under a zero data retention arrangement Anthropic does not store customer prompts or responses at rest once the API response is returned, and it applies to the Messages and Token Counting endpoints for the features marked eligible in the feature eligibility table. Eligibility is per feature rather than per endpoint, so a capability that rides on the same endpoint but requires storage to function falls outside the arrangement. The arrangement is also enabled per organization and does not automatically extend to other organizations under the same account, which makes checking both the feature table and the enabled scope part of any design review.

distractorNotes.b: Any usage in the Claude Console, including the playground, is explicitly outside the coverage even when the organization has the arrangement enabled.
distractorNotes.c: Code execution is named as a feature that rides on the messages endpoint but is not eligible, precisely because it requires storage to function.
distractorNotes.d: Cross-origin requests are not supported for organizations with this arrangement; browser-based applications have to route calls through a backend proxy server instead.

sourceNote: Sections "Zero data retention (ZDR)" (no storage of prompts or responses at rest after the response is returned; enabled per organization and not extended automatically to other organizations), "What ZDR covers" (Messages and Token Counting APIs for features listed as eligible) and "What ZDR does not cover" (Claude Console including playground, features riding on /v1/messages that are marked ineligible such as code execution, and CORS, for which requests must be routed through a backend proxy).

stem: A platform team keeps its build commands, review checklist, and naming conventions in a Claude Code instruction file. The guidance must reach everyone who clones the payments-api repository, travel with that repository in version control, and have no effect when the same developers work in their other repositories. Where should the file live?

options.text: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on each developer's machine, kept in step across the team by hand
CLAUDE.md at the repository root, or .claude/CLAUDE.md, committed to the repository
CLAUDE.local.md at the repository root, listed in .gitignore so it stays out of commits
A managed-policy CLAUDE.md deployed by IT to the operating system's system-wide location

explanation: Project scope is the only scope that is both repository-bound and shareable through source control. Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md from the working directory and every directory above it at launch, so a file committed at the repository root reaches every clone of that repository and nothing else. Project instructions are where build and test commands, coding standards, architectural decisions, and common workflows belong, because those are the things a new teammate would otherwise have to be told.

distractorNotes.a: This is user scope: it applies to one person across every project on that machine, and it cannot be version-controlled alongside the repository.
distractorNotes.c: This is local scope: personal, project-specific preferences that are deliberately gitignored, so teammates never receive them.
distractorNotes.d: Managed policy is organization-wide and applies in every repository. It also requires IT or device-management deployment, which is far broader than one repository's conventions.

sourceNote: Section "Choose where to put CLAUDE.md files": project instructions live at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, are for "Team-shared instructions for the project", and are "Shared with: Team members via source control". The same table scopes ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to "Just you (all projects)", ./CLAUDE.local.md to "Just you (current project)" with the advice to add it to .gitignore, and managed policy files to "All users in organization". Section "How CLAUDE.md files load" states that Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md "from your current working directory and every directory above it".

stem: A security team must guarantee that one Claude Code setting holds on every machine and cannot be changed by any developer. Separately, a developer wants a personal override for one project that is never committed to the repository. Select TWO statements that correctly describe how the configuration layers serve these two needs.

options.text: User-level configuration is the strongest of the layers a developer controls, because it describes the person rather than any particular project.
Configuration distributed centrally by the organisation cannot be overridden by any file a developer controls, which is what makes it fit for policy.
A key set at more than one layer is reported as a conflict at startup and ignored everywhere until someone removes the duplicate definitions.
Among the layers a developer controls, the more specific and local one wins, so an uncommitted personal file overrides the shared project file.
A value supplied for a single session is the weakest layer of all, so any configuration file present on disk will override it at run time.

explanation: The layers are ordered so that the two needs do not compete. Configuration an organisation distributes sits above everything an individual can edit, so it is the only layer that can carry a guarantee; anything a developer can edit, a developer can undo. Below that, precedence runs from the general to the specific, so a personal file scoped to one project beats the shared project file, which in turn beats the developer's global preferences. That ordering is what lets a personal override exist without weakening the policy above it.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Inverts the developer-controlled ordering. User-level settings are the broadest and most general of them, so they are overridden by project and project-local files rather than winning over them.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Setting a key at several layers is the normal case that precedence exists to resolve, not an error state. Refusing to apply the key would make layered configuration unusable.
distractorNotes.opt-e: Reverses the relationship. A value supplied for one session is the most specific expression of intent available, so it sits above the files on disk rather than beneath them.

sourceNote: Settings precedence figure, highest to lowest: 1. Managed settings (managed-settings.json, MDM, or the claude.ai console), 2. Command line (claude --settings), 3. Project local (.claude/settings.local.json), 4. Shared project (.claude/settings.json), 5. User (~/.claude/settings.json), summarized as "A key set at a higher level overrides the same key set lower down." The page's "Settings files and who they affect" table gives the scope of each file.

stem: A team runs Claude Code fully unattended inside a container with --dangerously-skip-permissions, which puts the session in bypassPermissions mode. Their security reviewer asks which of the permission rules configured in the repository's settings still have any force. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both deny and allow rules stop applying, because bypassPermissions skips the permission system in its entirety.
Allow rules keep pre-approving the tools they name, but deny rules are relaxed so the session can run without stopping.
Deny rules apply only until the first prompt would have been shown, after which the mode suppresses them for the rest of the session.
Deny rules still block in every mode, including bypassPermissions, while allow rules have no effect in that mode.

explanation: Permission modes set the baseline for what runs without asking, and permission rules layer on top of that baseline rather than being replaced by it. Deny rules are the part that survives everywhere: they block in every mode, bypassPermissions included, which is what makes a deny rule a dependable control rather than a convenience default. Allow rules are the mirror image and have no effect in bypassPermissions, because nothing there needs pre-approving. A short list of actions is auto-approved by no mode at all, including tools matched by an explicit ask rule, tools that require user interaction such as AskUserQuestion, and rm or rmdir removals targeting a critical path; in a -p run those few calls are denied rather than prompted. None of this makes the mode safe on its own, which is why it is documented as requiring a container, VM, or sandbox runtime.

distractorNotes.a: The mode skips the permission prompts, not the rule set. Deny rules are explicitly carved out as applying in every mode, and a handful of actions are auto-approved by no mode whatsoever.
distractorNotes.b: This inverts both halves. Allow rules are the ones rendered inert, since there is nothing left to pre-approve, and deny rules are the ones that keep applying.
distractorNotes.c: There is no first-prompt threshold. Deny rules are evaluated on every matching call for the whole session regardless of mode.

sourceNote: Section "Available modes": "Modes set the baseline. Layer permission rules on top to pre-approve or block specific tools. Deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions... Allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions." The carve-outs are listed under "Actions no mode auto-approves" (explicit ask rules, tools requiring user interaction such as AskUserQuestion, and rm/rmdir targeting a critical path), and the "Common setups" table notes that in a -p run the few calls that would still prompt are denied instead, with a container, VM, or sandbox runtime listed as required isolation.

stem: A platform team wants to ensure that Claude Code cannot execute certain destructive Bash commands across all developer workstations. Which approach provides the most robust and deterministic enforcement mechanism?

options.text: Configure a PreToolUse hook that evaluates the tool name and input, blocking the execution if a destructive command is detected.
Add instructions to the Claude Code system prompt explicitly forbidding the model from generating destructive commands.
Define an AgentRestriction policy in the Claude Code configuration file to disable the Bash tool for specific directories.
Modify the `.claudecodeignore` file to include all directories where destructive commands should be blocked.

explanation: Hooks in Claude Code, specifically PreToolUse hooks, allow developers to intercept and validate tool calls before they are executed. They provide a deterministic mechanism to enforce policies or block actions (such as exiting with a specific block code), making them the appropriate solution for robust security controls. By contrast, system prompts only provide soft guidance.

distractorNotes.b: System prompts provide "soft" guidance but do not deterministically guarantee that the model won't generate or attempt to run the command.
distractorNotes.c: Claude Code does not feature an "AgentRestriction" policy in its configuration for directory-specific tool disabling.
distractorNotes.d: The `.claudecodeignore` file prevents Claude Code from reading or indexing specific files, but it does not intercept or block terminal commands.

sourceNote: Section "Exit code output": "exit code 2 is the only exit code that blocks through the code alone. Without valid JSON on stdout, Claude Code treats exit code 1 as a non-blocking error and proceeds with the action, even though 1 is the conventional Unix failure code. If your hook is meant to enforce a policy, use exit 2." The same section states "The blocking message is the reason from your JSON's blocking decision when it makes one, and your stderr text otherwise" and that for PreToolUse the block stops the tool call; the exit-code-0 subsection notes a hook "can deny the call, but staying silent doesn't approve it"; the timeouts subsection states a hook that reaches its timeout is cancelled with its output discarded. The worked example blocks on exit 0 by printing a PreToolUse permissionDecision of "deny" as JSON.

stem: A development team is integrating Claude Code into their Continuous Integration (CI) pipeline to automate routine codebase tasks. Which TWO capabilities represent foundational features of Claude Code's headless operation that enable this automation? (Select TWO.)

options.text: It can execute autonomously without requiring human interaction or interactive terminal approvals.
It requires a developer to authenticate via an interactive browser prompt during every pipeline run.
It can produce structured machine-readable output, such as JSON, for downstream pipeline steps to easily parse.
It relies on a desktop graphical interface to orchestrate background CI tasks.
It automatically bypasses all organizational repository security constraints when run in CI environments.

explanation: Claude Code can operate in a 'headless' mode designed for automated environments like CI/CD pipelines. In this mode, it executes autonomously without requiring human interaction or interactive approvals (such as workspace trust dialogs). To facilitate integration, it can output structured, machine-readable formats like JSON, allowing downstream pipeline steps to easily parse and utilize the response. Non-interactive authentication is natively supported via environment variables.

distractorNotes.b: In automated environments, Claude Code uses non-interactive authentication methods (like environment variables containing API keys) rather than requiring an interactive browser login on every run.
distractorNotes.d: Claude Code is a CLI tool and its headless operation does not require a desktop graphical interface.
distractorNotes.e: Claude Code does not bypass security constraints; it operates securely within the permissions granted to the credentials or environment it runs under.

sourceNote: Section "Start faster with bare mode": --bare skips "auto-discovery of hooks, skills, custom commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md", is "useful for CI and scripts where you need the same result on every machine", and "In bare mode, Claude Code never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain. For the Anthropic API, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment ... or supply an apiKeyHelper in the --settings JSON." The same section warns that without --bare, "a -p session runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json and connects the servers in its .mcp.json", with "no workspace trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt". Section "Get structured output": --output-format accepts text (default), json ("structured JSON with result, session ID, and metadata", "with the text result in the result field"), and stream-json, which is streamed using --verbose and --include-partial-messages.

stem: A developer added a convention to a project CLAUDE.md, but Claude Code seems to ignore it. Before rewriting the wording, what is the most direct way to find out whether the file was actually loaded into the session?

options.text: Run /compact and read its summary, since compaction lists every instruction file it re-reads.
Run /context and look for the file under the memory files part of the breakdown.
Run /permissions to confirm that reading the instruction file is allowed.
Delete the user configuration directory and restart, since a stale cache is the usual cause.

explanation: The /context command shows everything occupying the context window for the current session, broken down by category, including memory files, so it is the first check for whether an instruction file is present at all. If the file is missing there, the cause is location: instruction files load from the working directory and its parents at launch, while a CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory loads only on demand when Claude reads a file in that directory with the Read tool. If /context shows the file did load, the problem is how the instruction is written, and the remedies are specificity, removing conflicting guidance, and keeping the file short. Targeted follow-ups are /memory, /skills, /hooks, /mcp, /permissions, /doctor, and /status, and a session started with customizations disabled isolates the surface responsible.

distractorNotes.a: Compaction summarizes the conversation to reclaim context. A project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk afterwards, but compaction reports no inventory of instruction files, so it answers nothing about what loaded at session start.
distractorNotes.c: Permission rules govern which tools Claude may use. They do not determine whether an instruction file is loaded into the session at startup.
distractorNotes.d: Deleting configuration is destructive and skips diagnosis. The documented isolation technique points a session at a separate, empty configuration directory instead of removing the real one.

sourceNote: Section "See what loaded into context": "The /context command shows everything occupying the context window for the current session, broken down by category: system prompt, system tools, MCP tools, custom subagents with the source each loaded from, memory files, skills, and conversation messages. Run it first to confirm whether your CLAUDE.md, rules, or skill descriptions are present at all." It adds that subdirectory CLAUDE.md files "load on demand when Claude reads a file in that directory with the Read tool, not at session start", and that when the file did load, "the issue is likely how the instruction is written rather than whether it loaded". The follow-up command table lists /memory, /skills, /hooks, /mcp, /permissions, /doctor, and /status, and "Test against a clean configuration" describes pointing CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR at an empty directory. The compaction behavior is stated at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory: "Project-root CLAUDE.md survives compaction: after /compact, Claude re-reads it from disk and re-injects it into the session."

scopeNote: Tests writing SMART success criteria to drive prompt iteration. The Domain 4 objective covers error type identification, recovery strategy selection, trace analysis, and isolating the integration layer from model output; defining success criteria is not among them. Siblings ccdv-f-0077/0078/0100 were rewritten into genuine error-diagnosis scenarios and correctly moved to core; this one and ccdv-f-0079 test the same success-criteria/methodology ground as originally-tagged ccdv-f-0076/0077/0078/0100 and were left untagged by oversight in the earlier pass.
stem: A team is about to begin prompt iteration on a support-ticket classifier. Which statement of success criteria is best suited to drive that work?

options.text: The classifier should handle the great majority of incoming tickets well and rarely frustrate customers, and is ready once the team agrees its output reads sensibly across a range of examples.

The classifier should lead every public text-classification benchmark by the end of the sprint, since an external leaderboard is objective, published, and directly comparable across competing approaches.
The classifier should reach an F1 score of at least 0.85 on a held-out set of 10,000 labelled tickets drawn from production traffic, a 5 percent improvement over the current baseline.
The classifier should reach an accuracy of at least 0.85 on the twenty examples the team used while drafting the prompt, re-measured after every prompt revision so that progress stays visible.

explanation: Useful success criteria are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant. This option names the metric and its threshold, states the dataset and its size, keeps that dataset held out and representative of the real distribution, and anchors the target to an improvement over the existing baseline so the goal is realistic. Criteria written this way can be tested empirically, which the prompt engineering guidance treats as a prerequisite before any prompt iteration begins.

distractorNotes.a: Neither specific nor measurable. Vague quality language gives nothing to grade against and no threshold separating a pass from a fail.
distractorNotes.b: Fails the achievable test. Targets should be grounded in industry benchmarks, prior experiments, research, or expert knowledge rather than set beyond current frontier capability, and public benchmarks may not be relevant to this application's own distribution.
distractorNotes.d: The examples used to author the prompt are not a held-out test set, so a high score shows fit to the drafting examples rather than generalization.

sourceNote: Section "Define your success criteria" states that good criteria are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, and Relevant, that achievable targets are based on "industry benchmarks, prior experiments, AI research, or expert knowledge", and that "Your success metrics should not be unrealistic to current frontier model capabilities." Its worked comparison rates "The model should classify sentiments well" as bad and, as good, "an F1 score of at least 0.85 (Measurable, Specific) on a held-out test set of 10,000 diverse Twitter posts (Relevant), which is a 5% improvement over the current baseline (Achievable)." The prerequisite of empirical testing is stated at https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview under "Before prompt engineering".

stem: While developing an application using the Anthropic API, a developer repeatedly encounters an HTTP 529 error during periods of high traffic. What does this specific error indicate, and how should the application respond?

options.text: It indicates an overloaded_error meaning Anthropic's API is temporarily overloaded; the application should retry the request with exponential backoff.
It indicates a rate_limit_error meaning the application has exceeded its allowed requests per minute; the application should prompt the user to upgrade their API tier.
It indicates an authentication_error meaning the API key is invalid or expired; the application must prompt the administrator to rotate the keys.
It indicates a request_too_large error meaning the prompt exceeded the context window; the application should automatically truncate the input text before retrying.

explanation: An HTTP 529 status code indicates an `overloaded_error`, which means Anthropic's API is temporarily experiencing high load. The recommended recovery strategy for this error type is to automatically retry the request using exponential backoff. This differs from a 429 `rate_limit_error`, which happens when the client exceeds their specific allotted rate limits.

distractorNotes.b: A rate limit error uses HTTP 429, not 529. While both might involve traffic limits, 529 is a server-side overload, whereas 429 is a client-side limit.
distractorNotes.c: An authentication error returns an HTTP 401. It is not related to high traffic or 529 errors.
distractorNotes.d: A request too large error returns an HTTP 413. It is caused by exceeding the token limit, not by periods of server-side high traffic.

sourceNote: Section "Eval design principles" lists exactly three: "Be task-specific: Design evals that mirror your real-world task distribution. Don't forget to factor in edge cases!" (listed edge cases include irrelevant or nonexistent input data, overly long input data or user input, poor, harmful, or irrelevant user input, and ambiguous test cases); "Automate when possible"; and "Prioritize volume over quality: More questions with slightly lower signal automated grading is better than fewer questions with high-quality human hand-graded evals." Section "Grade your evaluations" describes human grading as "Most flexible and high quality, but slow and expensive. Avoid if possible."

stem: A developer is building a classification application with Claude. During initial testing, they notice the model occasionally outputs invalid categories. Which TWO foundational debugging steps should they take to diagnose and resolve this issue? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Review the model's outputs and adjust the prompt to explicitly define the allowed categories.
Increase the temperature parameter to 1.0 to ensure the model explores all possible correct categories.
Set the top_p parameter to 0 to force the model to output the categories in alphabetical order.
Switch the API request from the Messages API to the legacy Text Completions API.
Add the failing examples to an evaluation test suite to systematically measure if prompt adjustments fix the issue.

explanation: When debugging unexpected model behavior such as incorrect categorization, foundational steps include reviewing the failures to refine prompt instructions (such as explicitly defining allowed categories) and adding those failing cases to an evaluation suite. A test suite allows developers to iterate on the prompt systematically, ensuring that changes resolve the errors without causing regressions.

distractorNotes.c: Increasing temperature increases randomness, which typically makes formatting and classification tasks less reliable.
distractorNotes.d: The top_p parameter controls nucleus sampling based on token probability; it does not sort outputs alphabetically.
distractorNotes.e: The Text Completions API is legacy. Switching to it is not recommended and will not inherently resolve instruction-following issues.

sourceNote: Section "Tips for LLM-based grading" gives three tips: "Have detailed, clear rubrics" (with the note that a use case "might require several rubrics for holistic evaluation"); "Empirical or specific: For example, instruct the LLM to output only 'correct' or 'incorrect', or to judge from a scale of 1-5. Purely qualitative evaluations are hard to assess quickly and at scale"; and "Encourage reasoning: Ask the LLM to reason first before producing an evaluation score, and then discard the reasoning. This increases evaluation performance." Section "Grade your evaluations" describes LLM-based grading as "Fast and flexible, scalable and suitable for complex judgment. Test to ensure reliability first then scale."

stem: A developer runs an exact-match evaluation to check if Claude correctly assigns one of four fixed labels to an input. The test continuously fails, despite manual spot-checks showing the model is generating the right words. What is the most appropriate first step to diagnose and resolve this test failure?

options.text: Inspect the raw outputs and update the evaluation script to normalize whitespace and casing before performing the exact match.
Replace the exact-match script with an LLM-as-a-judge prompt to flexibly evaluate the model's intended label.
Switch to manual human grading for all test cases, as automated string matching is too unreliable for categorical tasks.
Set the temperature to 0 to automatically prevent the model from generating any unexpected whitespace or capitalization.

explanation: When an exact-match evaluation for categorical answers produces false negatives, a foundational debugging step is to inspect the raw output for trivial discrepancies. Anthropic's guidance highlights that code-based grading is the fastest and most reliable method for clear-cut answers, but it typically requires comparing the output "after normalizing whitespace and case." Replacing the check with an LLM judge or human grading fails to address the root cause and introduces unnecessary cost and latency for a deterministic task.

distractorNotes.b: An LLM judge adds cost, latency, and variance. It is suitable for complex or subjective judgments, not for evaluating fixed, categorical labels.
distractorNotes.c: Human grading is the slowest and most expensive evaluation method. The guidance explicitly advises avoiding it when a simple, automated string match is possible.
distractorNotes.d: While setting temperature to 0 is recommended for classification tasks to reduce variance, it does not prevent the model from outputting spaces or capitalization. The output must still be normalized.

sourceNote: Section "Grade your evaluations": "When deciding which method to use to grade evals, choose the fastest, most reliable, most scalable method", ranking code-based grading first ("Fastest and most reliable, extremely scalable", examples "Exact match: output == golden_answer" and "String match: key_phrase in output"), human grading second ("slow and expensive. Avoid if possible"), and LLM-based grading third ("suitable for complex judgment"). The exact-match example eval states that such evals compare output with a predefined correct answer "typically after normalizing whitespace and case" and are "perfect for tasks with clear-cut, categorical answers".

scopeNote: Tests A/B comparison methodology (held-out set, fixed grader, multidimensional criteria) between two prompt versions. The Domain 4 objective covers error type identification, recovery strategy selection, trace analysis, and isolating the integration layer from model output; comparing prompt versions is not among them, the same reasoning applied to ccdv-f-0075.
stem: A candidate prompt, version two, is proposed to replace the prompt currently in production. Which TWO practices produce a trustworthy comparison between the two versions? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Change the model at the same time as the prompt, so that the strongest overall combination is found in a single evaluation pass.
Run both versions against the same held-out test set with the same grader and rubric, changing only the prompt between the runs.
Judge the outcome against the full set of success criteria, including operational measures such as latency and cost, rather than one headline metric.
Score version two on the examples that were used to write version two, since those examples express the intended behaviour more precisely than sampled production traffic does.
Adopt version two if a reviewer skims a handful of sampled outputs from each version and prefers what the new version produced.

explanation: Comparing versions is A/B testing against a baseline, which here is the earlier prompt. The difference is attributable to the prompt only if the dataset, the grader, and the rubric are held constant and the test set is held out from the work that produced the new version. The verdict should then be read against the multidimensional criteria the application actually needs, because most use cases require evaluation along several criteria at once, such as accuracy together with response time. A version that improves a headline score while regressing latency or cost is not necessarily an improvement, and where latency or cost is the failing criterion the better fix may be model selection rather than further prompt iteration.

distractorNotes.a: Changing two variables at once makes the result unattributable: any difference could come from the prompt, the model, or their interaction.
distractorNotes.d: Those examples are not held out. Scoring on the data used to author a prompt measures fit to that data rather than performance on the real distribution.
distractorNotes.e: An impression from a few samples is neither a defined metric nor a repeatable measurement, so it cannot establish whether the change is an improvement.

sourceNote: Section "Define your success criteria" lists A/B testing among quantitative methods as "Compare performance against a baseline model or earlier version", and anchors criteria to "a held-out test set". Its multidimensional example measures one use case on F1, non-toxicity, error severity, and 95% response time together, and states "Most use cases need multidimensional evaluation along several success criteria." Holding the dataset, grader, and rubric constant is the standard meaning of that A/B comparison rather than a separate quoted rule. The related overview at https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview adds that "Not every success criteria or failing eval is best solved by prompt engineering" and that latency and cost can sometimes be improved "by selecting a different model".

stem: An engineering manager wants to monitor Claude Code usage across their team and verify that the telemetry pipeline is functioning correctly. Which statement accurately describes the fundamental approach to configuring and verifying Claude Code telemetry?

options.text: Claude Code automatically sends telemetry to Anthropic's central dashboard; administrators verify the pipeline by checking the Anthropic console for active developer sessions.

Telemetry is strictly opt-in; administrators must explicitly configure Claude Code to export to their own OpenTelemetry collector and verify the setup by observing standard metrics or events on their backend.
Telemetry is enabled by default in enterprise deployments; administrators verify the pipeline by ensuring the proprietary Anthropic monitoring agent is running alongside Claude Code.
Administrators enable telemetry by aggregating local log files from each developer machine; the pipeline is verified by running a standard Claude Code command to print a summary of recent sessions.

explanation: Claude Code's telemetry is opt-in and natively integrates with standard OpenTelemetry backends rather than phoning home to Anthropic or requiring proprietary agents. Administrators must explicitly enable it and provide OTLP endpoint details. The pipeline is then verified on the organization's own backend by checking for expected initial metrics (like session counts) or logs (like user prompt events) rather than relying on an Anthropic dashboard or local log scraping.

distractorNotes.a: Claude Code does not send organizational telemetry to a central Anthropic dashboard; it exports to the organization's own configured OpenTelemetry backend.
distractorNotes.c: Telemetry is never enabled by default, and Claude Code natively supports OpenTelemetry without requiring a separate proprietary monitoring agent.
distractorNotes.d: Telemetry is exported over the network via OpenTelemetry protocols, not by manually aggregating local log files or running local summary commands.

sourceNote: Section "Quick start" shows CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 followed by separately chosen exporters (OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER and OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER, annotated "both are optional - configure only what you need") plus OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, and states "To verify a setup that exports metrics, check your backend for the claude_code.session.count metric, which Claude Code emits when a session starts. To verify a logs-only setup, submit a prompt and check for the claude_code.user_prompt event", with third-party exporter failures shown as "[3P telemetry]" errors under claude --debug. Section "Administrator configuration" shows the same keys inside the managed settings env block. Section "Standard attributes" states that event-only fields such as prompt.id "are never attached to metrics because they would cause unbounded cardinality". The client-side nature of per-run cost output is stated at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless, which calls total_cost_usd a client-side estimate that "can differ from your actual bill".

stem: A report generation job issues non-streaming Messages requests with a very large max_tokens value. Most calls succeed, but some fail after several minutes with no response body at all, and failures cluster on particular network paths. Which change matches the documented guidance?

options.text: Switch long generations to the streaming Messages API or the Message Batches API, since idle connections can be dropped.
Keep the non-streaming call and raise the client timeout, since the response is held server side until the client reconnects.
Treat the failures as a throughput limit and retry the identical non-streaming request with exponential backoff.
Lower max_tokens until responses return, since the failures show the requested ceiling exceeded the context window.

explanation: A non-streaming request holds one connection open for the entire generation, so a large max_tokens turns an ordinary call into a long-lived connection. Networks differ in reliability and some drop idle connections after a variable period, which is why the request can fail or time out without any response arriving. The documented remedies are to stream, so that data flows continuously and the client can process events as they arrive, or to use the Message Batches API, which lets the client poll for results instead of depending on an uninterrupted connection. Two supporting details are worth knowing: the official SDKs validate that a non-streaming request is not expected to exceed the service timeout, and they set a TCP keep-alive socket option, which a hand-rolled direct integration must arrange for itself. A request that does time out server side surfaces as a timeout error whose documented advice is likewise to move to streaming.

distractorNotes.b: There is no reconnect-and-collect mechanism for a dropped non-streaming call, so the partially generated response is simply lost. Extending the timeout does not help when an intermediary severs an idle connection.
distractorNotes.c: Throughput rejections arrive quickly with an explicit error, not as a silent multi-minute stall. Replaying the same non-streaming shape reproduces exactly the condition that failed.
distractorNotes.d: A max_tokens value larger than the model allows is rejected during validation, immediately and with an error. Failures that appear only after minutes of waiting point at connection duration instead.

sourceNote: Claude API errors - 'Long requests' section advising streaming or the Message Batches API for long-running requests, and noting dropped idle connections, SDK timeout validation, and TCP keep-alive

stem: A team is hardening the logging and failure handling of a direct HTTP integration that does not use an official SDK. Which practices match the documented guidance? Select TWO.

options.text: Record the request identifier header returned with every response so it can be quoted when escalating one call to support.
Correlate incidents by timestamp alone and treat the identifier as one value reused across a whole conversation.
Treat the set of error type values as open ended, because the values inside error objects may expand over time.
Read the identifier only from successful response bodies, since it is returned in the body rather than in a header.
Reject any response whose error type is not already known to the client, since only the documented type values are ever considered valid.

explanation: Two disciplines make a direct integration supportable. First, every response carries a request identifier header, and error bodies repeat the same value in a dedicated field; capturing it on successes as well as failures is what allows a specific call to be traced later, and support asks for it when investigating an individual request. Second, the error contract is explicitly open ended: the versioning policy allows the values inside error objects to expand, so the list of error type strings can grow. A parser that treats the enumeration as closed will break on an addition the contract permits. The safe handling for an unfamiliar type is neither to crash nor to retry blindly, since many conditions are permanent, but to fall through to a default that reports the failure with its identifier attached so a human can classify it.

distractorNotes.b: The identifier is unique per request, not per conversation, which is precisely what makes it useful for pinpointing one call. Timestamps alone cannot disambiguate concurrent requests.
distractorNotes.d: The identifier is returned as a response header on every response, and appears in the body only for errors. A client that looks solely at successful bodies will not find it.
distractorNotes.e: Hard failing on an unfamiliar type breaks the client on a change the contract expressly allows. Unknown types should fall through to a safe default that reports the failure for a human to classify.

sourceNote: Claude API errors - 'Request ID' section on the per-response identifier and quoting it to support, and 'Error shapes' section noting that values within error objects may expand under the versioning policy

stem: A development team is preparing to launch an application powered by the Claude API and is reviewing how rate limits will affect their production traffic. Which foundational statements about Claude API rate limits are correct? Select THREE.

options.text: Rate limits are measured using three distinct metrics: Requests Per Minute (RPM), Input Tokens Per Minute (ITPM), and Output Tokens Per Minute (OTPM).
Rate limits are shared globally across all Claude models, so heavy usage of one model reduces the available capacity for others.
When a rate limit is exceeded, the API returns a 429 Too Many Requests error, which developers should handle using exponential backoff or by honoring the Retry-After header.
Organization administrators can configure custom rate limits for individual Workspaces to prevent a single project from consuming the organization's entire API capacity.
Rate limits are only enforced based on the number of requests made; the length of the prompts and generated responses does not impact rate limiting.
Exceeding a rate limit will automatically trigger higher billing tiers, allowing the requests to succeed while charging an overage fee.

explanation: Claude API rate limits are enforced at the organization and workspace levels to ensure fair usage and system stability. They are measured using three distinct metrics: Requests Per Minute (RPM), Input Tokens Per Minute (ITPM), and Output Tokens Per Minute (OTPM). When an application exceeds any of these limits, the API returns a 429 error, which should be handled gracefully using retry logic or by observing the provided Retry-After header. To manage capacity effectively within a company, organization administrators can apply custom rate limits to individual Workspaces, ensuring that one runaway project does not exhaust the capacity available to other teams.

distractorNotes.b: Rate limits are applied per model (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet vs. Claude 3 Opus). Usage of one model does not consume the rate limit capacity of a different model.
distractorNotes.e: Rate limits consider both the number of requests (RPM) and the volume of text processed, measured in input and output tokens per minute (ITPM and OTPM).
distractorNotes.f: Exceeding a rate limit results in a 429 error (Too Many Requests) and temporary rejection of further requests, not automatic overage billing. Limits are increased by advancing through usage tiers, which requires a history of successful spend and payment.

sourceNote: Rate limits - 'About rate limits' bullets on the token bucket algorithm, enforcement over shorter intervals, and organization-level limits with user-configurable workspace limits, plus the 'Rate limits' section on RPM, ITPM, and OTPM and the retry-after header

stem: A production service starts receiving 429 responses. The failures persist for hours, the SDK's automatic retries never recover, and the responses carry no retry-after header. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The pinned version header has lapsed, so calls fail until the request is updated to a currently supported version value.
A transient acceleration condition applies, so retrying at a fixed interval until capacity returns is the correct response.
The organization reached its tier's monthly spend cap; the error details carry a spend limit code and access resumes later.
A spend limit the organization set for itself was reached, which is what a 429 with no retry-after header indicates.

explanation: Reaching a usage tier's monthly spend cap pauses API usage and returns the same 429 status and rate limit error type as an ordinary throughput rejection, which is why it is so often misdiagnosed. Two signals separate them. The spend cap response carries no retry-after header, so backoff has nothing to honor and both hand-written retries and the SDK's automatic ones keep failing. The error details also carry a specific spend limit error code that a client can branch on to raise an alert instead of retrying. Recovery comes from moving to a higher tier or from the start of the next month, not from waiting a few seconds. A limit the organization sets for itself behaves differently and is returned as a 400 invalid request error, which is another reason to inspect the error body rather than the status code alone.

distractorNotes.a: A version problem is reported as a request validation failure, not as a 429. Pinned versions do not silently lapse and start returning throughput errors.
distractorNotes.b: Acceleration conditions do arise from sharp usage increases, but they are transient and are addressed by ramping traffic gradually. They do not produce hours of failures immune to backoff.
distractorNotes.d: A spend limit the organization configures for itself is returned as a 400 invalid request error rather than a 429, so this misreads the status code and would send the team to the wrong setting.

sourceNote: Rate limits - 'Reaching your spend cap' subsection describing the 429 rate_limit_error with no retry-after header and a spend limit error code, contrasted with the 400 returned for a self-configured spend limit

stem: An organization is building multiple distinct applications using the Anthropic API. They want to separate each application's resources, manage API keys independently, and set individual spend limits while maintaining centralized billing. Which Anthropic Console feature should they use to achieve this?

options.text: Organizations, which provide separate billing accounts for each application.
Workspaces, which separate projects and environments under a single billing account.
Projects, which isolate API keys and prompt templates per team member.
Environments, which automatically separate development and production traffic.

explanation: Workspaces are designed to separate projects, environments, and teams while keeping billing and administration centralized. Each workspace can have its own API keys, rate limits, and monthly spend caps, making them the foundational tool for managing multiple integrations safely within a single organization.

distractorNotes.a: While organizations separate resources, they create entirely separate billing accounts, which does not meet the requirement for centralized billing.
distractorNotes.c: Projects are a feature within the Claude web interface (Claude.ai) for organizing chats and knowledge, not a console feature for API resource management.
distractorNotes.d: While workspaces are often used to separate development and production, 'Environments' is not a distinct Anthropic Console feature for resource separation.

sourceNote: Workspaces - 'How workspaces work' on separating projects and environments and on keys scoped to a single workspace, plus 'Set workspace limits' and the 'Archive a workspace' warning that archiving is irreversible and archives the workspace's keys

stem: An architect is deciding whether a feature currently offered in beta can carry a long-lived production workload. Which statements about beta features are accurate? Select THREE.

options.text: Beta features can undergo breaking changes with notice, and they can also be deprecated or removed entirely.
Pinning an API version extends the same compatibility guarantees to beta features as it does to stable ones.
An unrecognized or unauthorized beta name is ignored, so the request simply proceeds without that feature.
Only one beta feature can be enabled per request, so betas have to be adopted strictly one at a time.
A beta feature may carry rate limits or pricing that differ from the generally available surface.
A beta feature may be unavailable in some regions, so availability has to be checked for each deployment.

explanation: Betas give early access to experimental capability, and the documentation is explicit about what that costs. A beta may change in a breaking way with notice, may be deprecated or removed, may have different rate limits or pricing, and may not be available in every region. Each of those is a distinct planning risk, so depending on a beta in a long-lived system means budgeting for migration work and verifying regional availability wherever the workload runs. Mechanically, a beta is enabled by naming it in the dedicated beta header, using the exact documented name, which conventionally embeds a release date; the SDKs send that header when the feature names are supplied through their beta parameter. Several betas can be enabled at once by listing their names together in the header, and some beta APIs additionally require a feature-specific header on every request to their endpoints.

distractorNotes.b: The compatibility guarantees attached to a pinned version cover the stable surface. Beta features sit outside them, which is the whole reason the warnings about breaking changes exist.
distractorNotes.c: An invalid beta name, or one the organization cannot access, is rejected with a request validation error. Requests do not quietly fall back to behavior without the feature.
distractorNotes.d: Multiple betas can be enabled on the same request by listing their names together, so features need not be adopted one at a time.

sourceNote: Beta headers - the warning listing that beta features may have breaking changes with notice, be deprecated or removed, have different rate limits or pricing, and not be available in all regions, plus 'Multiple beta features' and 'Error handling'

stem: A product owner writes that a new assistant simply has to feel fast. Before the team can build against that, the requirement must be restated in terms it can measure. Which statements reflect the documented guidance on latency? Select TWO.

options.text: Latency targets should be fixed before prompt quality is explored, since no quality work can start until they are met.
Time to first token and time to a complete response are separate measures, and the requirement must say which it binds.
Capping the output ceiling is a precise way to hit a latency target, because generation is trimmed at a clean boundary.
Streaming returns output before generation finishes, improving perceived responsiveness rather than total generation time.
Once streaming is enabled the two latency measures converge, so only a single number needs to be tracked afterwards.

explanation: Feeling fast is not one quantity. Baseline latency covers processing the prompt and producing the response, while time to first token measures only how long the user waits before anything appears, and the two move independently. A requirement that does not say which one it constrains cannot be verified, and it also cannot be designed against, because the levers differ: trimming input and output length and choosing a faster model move total time, whereas streaming mainly moves the perceived figure by letting output appear while generation continues. Naming the measure is therefore the first step in turning the request into something testable. The guidance also warns against sequencing this work wrongly: engineer a prompt that performs well first, then apply latency reduction, because optimizing for speed too early can hide what good performance would have looked like.

distractorNotes.a: This inverts the recommended order. Establishing quality first and reducing latency afterwards is advised, since premature constraints can prevent the team from discovering top performance.
distractorNotes.c: An output ceiling is described as a blunt instrument. It cuts generation wherever it lands, possibly mid-sentence, so it usually requires post-processing rather than delivering a clean result.
distractorNotes.e: The two stay distinct under streaming, which is exactly when the distinction matters most: first output can appear quickly while the complete response still takes just as long to finish.

sourceNote: Reducing latency - 'How to measure latency' section defining baseline latency and time to first token, the 'Stream responses' section on improved perceived responsiveness, and the opening note advising latency reduction only after prompt quality is established

stem: A service assembles prompts dynamically from retrieved documents, so request size varies and sometimes approaches the model's context window. The team wants to handle overflow correctly rather than discovering it in production. How does the API behave when a request exceeds the context window?

options.text: Any request whose input plus max_tokens exceeds the window is refused up front on every model, so a preflight count is strictly mandatory.
Input that alone exceeds the window is always refused with a 400, while input plus max_tokens over the limit may instead be accepted and stopped mid-generation.
Overflowing input is silently truncated from the oldest messages, so requests still succeed but the earliest conversation turns quietly disappear from what the model actually sees.
Overflow surfaces only in the usage field after the fact, so neither a request error nor any distinct stop reason is ever produced for it.

explanation: There are two distinct overflow paths. If the input alone already exceeds the context window, the API returns a 400 invalid_request_error reporting that the prompt is too long, and this holds on every model. If the input fits but input plus max_tokens exceeds the window, recent model generations accept the request and, if generation actually reaches the limit, end it with stop_reason model_context_window_exceeded; earlier generations return a validation error instead unless a beta header opts them into that behavior. Because the second path produces a successful but incomplete response, clients must inspect the stop reason rather than assume completion, and the documented preventive measure is estimating usage with the token counting API before sending.

distractorNotes.a: This over-generalizes the strict case. On recent model generations a request whose input fits but whose input plus max_tokens does not is accepted and simply stops at the limit with a dedicated stop reason, so it is not universally refused up front.
distractorNotes.c: Rolling first-in-first-out context management is described as a chat interface behavior and is explicitly distinguished from standard API behavior. The API does not silently drop earlier turns; input that is oversized by itself is rejected.
distractorNotes.d: Both an error path and a stop reason exist: a 400 invalid_request_error for input that is too long by itself, and model_context_window_exceeded when generation reaches the limit. Usage reporting is not the only signal available.

sourceNote: Sections 'Context window overflow behavior' (400 invalid_request_error for oversized input; stop_reason model_context_window_exceeded on newer models; token counting to stay within limits) and 'How the context window works' (footnote distinguishing chat interface rolling behavior).

stem: An interactive assistant feels sluggish to its users, and the team is applying Anthropic's guidance on reducing latency. Which THREE statements reflect that guidance? Select THREE.

options.text: Baseline latency covers processing the prompt and generating the whole response, while time to first token measures only the first token's arrival.
Streaming improves perceived responsiveness because the interface can display and process output as it arrives.
Raising temperature is the documented way to shorten responses, because added randomness makes the model reach its conclusion sooner.
Reaching max_tokens ends a response gracefully at the nearest sentence boundary, which makes it the preferred way to shorten prose answers without post-processing.
Latency work should come before prompt quality is established, so quality is never tuned on a needlessly slow configuration.
Asking for a paragraph or sentence limit beats asking for an exact word count because models count tokens rather than words.

explanation: The guidance separates two measurements: baseline latency is the time taken to process the prompt and generate the response, whereas time to first token measures only how long the first token takes to appear after the prompt was sent, which is the metric that matters most when streaming. Streaming lets the model start returning its response before the full output is complete, which significantly improves perceived responsiveness because the interface can update in real time while other work proceeds in parallel. And because language models count tokens rather than words, asking for an exact word count is less effective than asking for a paragraph or sentence limit when the goal is shorter, faster output.

distractorNotes.c: The guidance runs the other way: lower temperature values can lead to more focused and shorter responses, while higher values may produce more diverse and potentially longer ones. Temperature is presented as something to experiment with, not a dependable length control.
distractorNotes.d: When a response reaches max_tokens it is cut off, possibly mid-sentence or mid-word. It is described as a blunt technique that may require post-processing and suits multiple choice or short answers rather than prose.
distractorNotes.e: The recommended order is the opposite: engineer a prompt that works well without model or prompt constraints first, then apply latency reduction, because optimizing prematurely can prevent you from discovering what top performance looks like.

sourceNote: Opening note on engineering the prompt before reducing latency, section 'How to measure latency' (baseline latency versus time to first token), and section 'How to reduce latency' subsections '2. Optimize prompt and output length' and '3. Stream responses'.

stem: A team is sizing max_tokens and forecasting spend for a workload that runs with thinking enabled, and wants the token accounting right before it ships. How are thinking tokens accounted for?

options.text: They are budgeted separately from max_tokens, so that parameter constrains only the visible response text that follows the reasoning.
They are excluded from rate limit accounting because they are internal reasoning rather than content returned to the caller.
They never count toward the context window because the API automatically removes them from conversation history on every model.
They are a subset of max_tokens, are billed as output tokens, and count toward both the context window and rate limits.

explanation: Thinking tokens are drawn from the same max_tokens allowance as the response text, are billed as output tokens once at the moment they are generated, and count toward rate limits and the context window like any other tokens in the request. Two consequences matter for forecasting. First, with adaptive thinking the model allocates its own thinking budget, so usage varies from request to request and a single sample is a poor basis for a budget. Second, whether prior thinking blocks remain in conversation history is model-dependent: where they are retained they become part of later requests' input and are billed as input tokens along with the rest of the history, whereas where the API strips them they stop consuming the window on later turns.

distractorNotes.a: Thinking tokens are documented as a subset of the max_tokens parameter rather than a separate allowance, so a budget that overlooks them can be largely consumed by reasoning before the response text is finished.
distractorNotes.b: Thinking tokens count toward rate limits in addition to being billed as output tokens. Treating them as invisible internal work understates both the spend and the throughput a workload consumes.
distractorNotes.c: Stripping of previous thinking blocks is a per-model default rather than universal, and models that keep them continue to count and bill those blocks as input tokens. In every case the tokens counted toward the window during the turn that generated them.

sourceNote: Section 'The context window with thinking': thinking tokens are part of max_tokens, billed as output, count toward rate limits, and have model-dependent preservation.

stem: An internal service desk receives requests that fall into a few clearly distinct categories, such as password resets, hardware faults, and software licence approvals. Each category is handled best by its own prompt, tools, and downstream process, and the category can be identified reliably from the request itself. Which documented agentic pattern fits this design?

options.text: Routing: classify the incoming request, then direct it to a specialized follow-up task built for that category.
Prompt chaining: pass every request through the same fixed sequence of steps, with each step consuming the previous step's output.
Parallelization using voting: run the same request several times in parallel and aggregate the outputs into one answer.
Evaluator-optimizer: have one call draft a response and a second call critique it in a loop until the critique is satisfied.

explanation: Routing classifies an input and sends it to a specialized follow-up task. Its value is separation of concerns: without it, one prompt has to serve every category, and tuning that prompt for one request type can degrade performance on others. Routing fits tasks with distinct categories that are better handled separately and where classification can be performed accurately, whether by a model or a conventional classifier.

distractorNotes.b: Prompt chaining decomposes one task into a fixed sequence and trades latency for accuracy. It does not address different categories needing different handlers.
distractorNotes.c: Voting runs the same task several times to gain confidence from diverse outputs, which suits judgement calls rather than dispatch. A reliably identifiable category needs one specialized handler, not repeated attempts at the same one.
distractorNotes.d: Evaluator-optimizer pairs a generator with a critic in an iterative refinement loop. It improves one response rather than selecting a specialized handler.

sourceNote: Section 'Building blocks, workflows, and agents', subsection 'Workflow: Routing'

stem: An organization is deploying an autonomous agent using the Agent SDK and wants to ensure that the agent operates safely and transparently. They plan to use hooks to enforce security policies. Which TWO of the following statements accurately reflect the high-level purpose and capabilities of hooks in this ecosystem?

options.text: Hooks can intercept a tool call before it executes, providing an intervention point to enforce guardrails or require human-in-the-loop approval for sensitive operations.
The post-tool-use hook is the primary mechanism for preventing unauthorized actions, as it evaluates the tool's output to determine if the execution should be rolled back.
Organizations can use hooks to establish a comprehensive audit trail by observing both the model's intended action prior to execution and the actual outcome returned by the tool.
Hooks enhance security by directly modifying the underlying LLM's behavioral safeguards, permanently teaching the model which tool calls are prohibited within the environment.
When a hook pauses for human approval, it suspends all background processes globally across the SDK infrastructure to ensure the system state remains frozen.
Hooks are designed to replace traditional Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls, allowing the agent to dynamically provision and revoke its own system permissions.

explanation: Hooks are a foundational security and safety feature in the Agent SDK, designed to provide visibility and control over an agent's actions. Pre-tool hooks intercept requests before execution to enforce guardrails or human-in-the-loop approvals. The combination of pre- and post-tool hooks allows developers to comprehensively audit both what the model attempted to do and what the tool actually produced. Hooks operate at the application layer and do not alter model weights, replace system-level IAM, or globally freeze infrastructure.

distractorNotes.b: Post-tool hooks trigger after a tool has already executed. They can modify what is returned to the model, but they cannot prevent the action from occurring or automatically roll back state changes.
distractorNotes.d: Hooks provide runtime guardrails and feedback within the application layer. They do not modify the underlying foundational model's weights or permanently alter its internal safeguards.
distractorNotes.e: Hooks pause the execution flow of the specific agent or session they are attached to. They do not implement a global freeze of all processes or infrastructure.
distractorNotes.f: Hooks complement existing security architectures by adding agent-specific application-level controls. They do not replace underlying infrastructure controls like IAM.

sourceNote: Sections 'How hooks work' and 'Available hooks'; 'Configure hooks' subsection 'Matchers'; 'Callback functions' subsections 'Inputs' and 'Outputs'

stem: A backend service is written in a language other than Python or TypeScript. The team wants the same agent loop the Claude Agent SDK provides, does not want to implement tool execution and the result feedback cycle themselves, and requires the loop to run on infrastructure they operate. What does the documentation direct them to do?

options.text: Use the Client SDK for their language, which exposes the same agent loop through a native binding to the harness.
Adopt Managed Agents, which is the language-agnostic form of the Agent SDK and exposes the same agent loop over HTTP.
Reimplement the agent loop against the Messages API directly, since no supported option exists outside of the Python and TypeScript SDKs.
Run the Claude Code command line interface as a subprocess in print mode with JSON output, and drive it from their service.

explanation: The Agent SDK is available as a library for Python and TypeScript only. The documented way to drive the same agent loop from another language is to run the command line interface as a subprocess, using the print flag with the JSON output format so the calling service can parse structured results. This keeps tool execution, context management, and the loop itself inside the harness while running on the team's own infrastructure. The comparison of Anthropic's agent-building options separates this case from the alternatives: a library that runs the loop in your own process, a terminal interface for interactive use, a client library for calling the API directly, and a hosted service.

distractorNotes.a: The Client SDK gives direct access to the Anthropic API rather than to the Claude Code harness, and choosing it means implementing the tool loop yourself, which is the work this team wants to avoid.
distractorNotes.b: Managed Agents is a separate hosted product rather than another distribution of the Agent SDK. Anthropic runs the agent and its sandbox, which does not satisfy a requirement to run the loop on infrastructure the team operates.
distractorNotes.c: A supported option does exist, so reimplementing the loop is unnecessary; it would also move tool execution, context management, and error handling back into application code.

sourceNote: Section 'Compare the Agent SDK to other Claude tools'

stem: A content team needs generated policy summaries to be checked against a fixed rubric before publication, and auditors must be able to see what the first draft looked like and why it changed. The engineer is deciding whether to keep the work in one request or split it into an explicit chain of separate API calls. Which reasoning matches Anthropic's guidance on chaining complex prompts?

options.text: Chain the work, because a task with more than one reasoning step cannot be completed within a single request and must be decomposed into separate calls, one per step, before the model can attempt it at all.

Keep the work in one request and separate the draft, review, and refine stages with tags, because splitting the task into separate calls discards everything produced in the earlier stages and forces a restart from scratch.

Chain the work, because chaining is what gives you an inspectable intermediate output and a defined pipeline; the documented shape is draft, then review against explicit criteria, then refine, each step its own call.

Chain the work mainly to reduce cost, because several short requests process fewer total tokens than one longer request that has to carry the draft and the rubric through to the end of a single response.

explanation: Current guidance is that much multistep reasoning is handled inside a single response, so chaining is no longer the default answer to task complexity. What chaining still buys you is control at the seams: it is called out as useful specifically when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a particular pipeline structure. The documented canonical pattern is self-correction, meaning generate a draft, review it against criteria, then refine based on that review, with each step issued as a separate API call so the run can be logged, evaluated, or branched at any point. That is exactly the requirement here, since the rubric check must be a distinct auditable stage and the original draft has to remain visible.

distractorNotes.a: This overstates the need for chaining. Multistep reasoning is largely handled within a single response, which is why the guidance now frames chaining as a control and observability technique rather than a capability workaround.
distractorNotes.b: Separate calls do not discard earlier work; the draft and the review are passed forward as input to the next call. Keeping everything in one request is what removes the inspection point the team needs.
distractorNotes.d: Cost is not a documented rationale for chaining. Splitting a task does not inherently reduce the total tokens processed, since each call still has to carry the context it needs, and the stated reasons to chain are inspection of intermediate outputs and pipeline control.

sourceNote: Chain complex prompts section: explicit prompt chaining remains useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure, and the most common chaining pattern is self-correction, generating a draft, reviewing it against criteria, then refining, with each step as a separate API call so you can log, evaluate, or branch.

stem: A developer is planning to use the Claude API's native Structured Outputs feature to extract specific data from unstructured text into JSON. Which TWO statements accurately describe the foundational capabilities of this feature? (Select TWO.)

options.text: It guarantees that the output will be parseable JSON that strictly adheres to the required fields and data types defined in the schema.
It guarantees both structural validity and factual accuracy, preventing the model from hallucinating incorrect data within the JSON values.
It eliminates the need for prompt engineering, as the provided schema fully replaces the need to describe the task in the system prompt.
It can be used to generate standalone JSON responses, and it also powers strict schema enforcement for Tool Use inputs.
It handles schema violations by automatically retrying the generation on the Anthropic backend until the model produces valid JSON.
It is only available when using Tool Use, requiring developers to define a dummy tool even if they only want a standard JSON response.

explanation: The Structured Outputs feature uses constrained decoding to ensure that the model's output strictly adheres to a provided JSON schema. This guarantees well-formed JSON, correct data types, and the presence of required fields natively during the generation process (Option A). Furthermore, this feature is versatile: it can be used independently for standard JSON generation, and it also powers strict schema enforcement for Tool Use inputs (Option D).

distractorNotes.b: Structured Outputs enforce the syntax and type structure of the output, but the model can still hallucinate or extract factually incorrect values within those structural fields.
distractorNotes.c: While the schema defines the structure, developers still need to use prompt engineering to instruct the model on what data to extract and how to populate the schema.
distractorNotes.e: The feature does not rely on automatic backend retries. Instead, it uses constrained decoding to guarantee valid JSON structurally on the first pass, effectively eliminating the need for retries due to schema violations.
distractorNotes.f: Structured Outputs and strict tool use are complementary features. You can use Structured Outputs for standard JSON responses entirely independently of Tool Use.

sourceNote: How SDK transformation works subsection: the SDK helpers remove unsupported constraints such as minimum, maximum, minimum length and maximum length, move the constraint info into the description, add additional properties false to all objects, filter string formats, and validate responses against the original schema, so the model receives a simplified schema while application code still enforces all constraints; the Why use structured outputs section states that constrained decoding yields always-valid, type-safe output with guaranteed required fields and no retries for schema violations, and the introduction describes JSON outputs and strict tool use as complementary features usable independently or together.

stem: A platform team's agent has grown to several hundred tools spanning many integrations. Definitions now consume a large share of the context window before any work begins, and the agent increasingly picks the wrong tool. The team adds the tool search tool and marks most definitions for deferred loading. Select THREE statements that correctly describe how this arrangement works.

options.text: Every tool definition still travels in the request's tools array; deferred loading marks which of them stay out of the initial context rather than removing them from the request.
Deferred tools are retrieved from an external tool registry at call time, so their schemas no longer need to be supplied with the request and the tools array shrinks to the non-deferred set.
At least one tool must remain non-deferred, normally the tool search tool itself, because something has to be present initially in order to surface the deferred definitions.
Deferring a tool changes where it executes, routing its calls to Anthropic's infrastructure instead of the application that defined it, which no longer runs it.
When a search matches, the API returns references to the matching tools and expands them into full definitions, after which Claude calls the discovered tool in the ordinary way.
The gain is limited to latency, since the definitions still occupy the same amount of context once the request has been assembled, regardless of which tools are used.

explanation: Tool search addresses two problems that arrive together as a tool library grows: definitions crowd the context window, and selection accuracy falls away once several dozen tools are simultaneously available. The mechanism is discovery, not relocation. The application continues to declare every tool it owns, deferred loading keeps the marked ones out of the initial system prompt, and at least one non-deferred tool has to remain so that a search can happen at all. A matching search returns references that the API expands into full definitions on the spot, so only the handful of tools relevant to the current request ever reach the model's context.

distractorNotes.b: There is no external registry in this design. Schemas are still supplied in full with the request, which is what allows the API to expand a match into a complete definition without another round trip.
distractorNotes.d: Deferred loading affects only when a definition enters the model's context. It leaves the execution boundary untouched, so a client tool that is deferred still executes in the application when it is eventually called.
distractorNotes.f: Reducing the context consumed by definitions is the primary purpose. Loading only the few tools a request actually needs cuts the definition footprint substantially and is what keeps selection accuracy from degrading across a large library.

sourceNote: Tool search tool — the 'Context bloat' and 'Tool selection accuracy' points in the introduction, and 'How tool search works'

stem: A team is designing a Model Context Protocol server for an internal knowledge platform. They need three things: read-only document sources that the host application selects and supplies as context, a small set of actions the model may invoke on its own initiative, and named starting templates that a person chooses from a menu. Which mapping onto the server's building blocks is correct?

options.text: The documents are resources, but resources are model-controlled in the same way tools are, so the model pulls them in whenever it judges them relevant and the host makes no selection.
